outline.chapter_title: Section 2(d) of the Lanham Act and TTAB Appellate Review
outline.description: Introduces the statutory bar to registration based on likelihood of confusion, explains how opposition proceedings work at the TTAB, and sets out the Federal Circuit’s standards of review that frame appellate outcomes in TTAB cases.
subtopics: The text, purpose, and policy of 15 U.S.C. § 1052(d) (likelihood of confusion as a registration bar)
Anatomy of TTAB proceedings: applications, intent-to-use filings, publication, letters of protest, and oppositions
Party roles and burdens: opposer’s burden, applicant’s responses, evidentiary burdens at the Board
Standard of review on appeal: de novo review of legal conclusions vs substantial-evidence review of TTAB factfinding
The legal significance of goods/services identifications and priority in the registration system
Standard character vs word/design marks: scope of protection and what is compared
Using the Trademark ID Manual and dictionaries to construe identifications
Financial services landscape basics (banks, card issuers, program managers) relevant to trademark relatedness analyses

outline.description: Surveys the thirteen DuPont factors, how courts and the TTAB weigh them, and the doctrinal development of the most frequently dispositive factors, with special emphasis on the second, sixth, and first factors that are central to the case study.
subtopics: Overview of the thirteen DuPont factors and the interdependence principle
Weighting and flexibility: not all factors are relevant or equal in every case
Factor 2 (similarity of goods/services): relatedness, partial legal identity, channels of trade, classes of consumers
Evidence under Factor 2: third-party registrations showing single-source offerings; marketplace practices
Factor 6 (number and nature of similar marks on similar goods): crowded field doctrine; conceptual vs commercial strength
What counts as “similar goods”: identical vs similar; Olde Tyme Foods and Juice Generation guidance
Evidence under Factor 6: third-party registrations vs marketplace use; the role of quantity and context (Jack Wolfskin, Juice Generation)
Factor 1 (similarity of the marks): appearance, sound, connotation, overall commercial impression; the effect of mark strength on this analysis
Interplay among Factors 1, 2, and 6: how strength and marketplace context modulate perceived similarity

outline.chapter_title: Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp.: A Case Study in Applying DuPont
outline.description: Walks through the Federal Circuit’s opinion as a vehicle to learn how to apply DuPont, highlighting how correct and incorrect factor analyses affect the likelihood-of-confusion determination.
subtopics: Factual background: parties, services, and the marks (ASPIRE vs ASPIRE BANK word/design); industry context
Procedural posture: examination, protest, publication, opposition, TTAB decision, and Federal Circuit appeal
Factor 2 affirmed: construing “credit card services” and “banking and financing services”; partial legal identity; third-party registrations showing co-provision of services (Coach Services)
Factor 6 vacated: Board’s erroneous narrowing of “similar goods” to only credit card services despite finding highly similar services under Factor 2
Consistency principle emerging from Apex: the scope of similarity adopted under one DuPont factor should inform others
Factor 1 vacated: commercial impression analysis must account for any change in perceived strength after a proper Factor 6 analysis (I.AM.Symbolic linkage)
Standards of review in action: substantial evidence supporting Factor 2 vs legal error driving vacatur on Factors 6 and 1
Use of authorities: Coach Services, Juice Generation, Jack Wolfskin, Olde Tyme Foods, and their roles in the court’s reasoning
Outcome and remedy: affirm-in-part, vacate-in-part, remand; costs to appellant

outline.chapter_title: Proving and Refuting Likelihood of Confusion at the TTAB
outline.description: Provides a practice-oriented guide to building the evidentiary record on key DuPont factors, using Apex Bank as a roadmap for what works, what fails, and how to preserve issues for appeal.
subtopics: Building Factor 2 evidence: dictionaries, industry reports, expert testimony, and third-party registrations to show relatedness and partial identity
Third-party registrations as probative of single-source provision and channels of trade: when and how they matter
Building Factor 6 evidence: assembling and authenticating marketplace uses; distinguishing registrations from use; what makes a field “crowded”
Quantitative and qualitative showings under Factor 6: numbers, market prominence, geographic scope, duration, and consumer exposure
Defining the relevant public and the universe of similar goods/services without improperly narrowing scope
Conceptual vs commercial strength: dictionary meanings (e.g., laudatory terms), descriptiveness spectrum, and proof of marketplace recognition
Factor 1 proof: visuals, specimens, sound comparisons, connotation evidence; how strength and marketplace context influence commercial impression
Procedural mechanics: notices of reliance, testimony declarations, website evidence, hearsay pitfalls, and preserving objections
Maintaining analytical consistency across factors and arguments; avoiding the Apex error on scope of similarity
Appellate preservation: tying record evidence to specific DuPont factors and articulating legal vs factual challenges

outline.description: Assesses the doctrinal significance of Apex Bank, offers guidance for practitioners and students, and situates the decision within the broader trademark landscape for financial services and beyond.
subtopics: Key takeaway: uniform scope of “similarity” should guide multiple DuPont factors once the Board finds highly similar or partially identical services
Predicted impact on TTAB practice: expanded consideration of third-party use across related service categories under Factor 6
Financial services implications: house marks plus industry descriptors (e.g., “BANK”) and how crowded-field showings may narrow protection
Reconciling ID Manual changes with evidence of actual marketplace practices
Strategy checklist for opposers and applicants post-Apex
Classroom hypotheticals: varying numbers of third-party uses; narrower identifications; stylized vs standard-character comparisons
Comparative notes: TTAB appeals to the Federal Circuit vs civil actions under § 1071(b); deference to Board factfinding
Exam and practice takeaways: structuring a DuPont analysis; integrating factor interdependence; spotting legal vs factual appellate issues
